power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p ≥ 0.22", Text = "Excluding members whose birth name was not known (H2a: 1.68, 0.81-3.47; H2b: 1.00, 0.81-1.22), cutting the cabinet lists at the end of 2024, and removing 73 members born on 1 January or 1 to 3 April (all p ≥ 0.22) did not change the results; every confidence interval includes 1."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 35 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: A positive control, the relative-age effect among Olympic football and ice-hockey players, was detected with the same data and methods (30.0% born January-March against 24.7% of days; p = 1.8 × 10 ²⁴).

Among 111,447 legislators in the 160 countries with variation in the outcome, the 1,398 heads of state or government were not more likely to have a leadership Life Path number (24.5% against 26.1%; H1: OR 0.90, 0.79-1.03, p = 0.13) or Expression number (20.5% against 22.3%; H2: 0.88, 0.76-1.01, p = 0.064).

Of 1,385 leaders with a recorded start date, 11.91% took office in Personal Year 1, against 11.36% expected (H3a: +0.55 pp, -0.65 to +1.73; p = 0.39).

Of 62,914 deceased legislators, 11.27% died in Personal Year 9, against 11.11% expected (H3b: +0.16 pp, -0.08 to +0.41; p = 0.20); the difference lies within the preregistered ±1-point equivalence margin (TOST p = 6.7 × 10 ¹²).

The sitelinks gradient, however, remains after the identification indicator is added (OR 2.48), and the indicator itself is not significant in that model (p = 0.088).

In Japan both registered conditions hold: in the 165 trials without identification the hit rate (25.5%) was not shown to be above 0.20 (p = 0.052), and the judge chose marked summaries twice as often as at random (7.0% against 3.6%; p = 0.007).
The positive control shows that the null results are not the product of an insensitive design: the same data and methods detected the relative-age effect at p = 1.8 × 10 ²⁴.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Execution
**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 45 scripts: 17 ran without error, 18 errored, 2 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 3 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: fa42s_compute.py (by fa42s_validate.py); studies3_4_code_results.zip/fa42s_compute.py (by analyse_th45d.py, analyse_th45d_ci.py, compute_de440.py, compute_s3.py, deviation_ci.py, deviation_s3_events.py); lon_ae.py (by analyse_th45d.py, analyse_th45d_ci.py, compute_de440.py, compute_s3.py, deviation_ci.py, deviation_s3_events.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`). **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `analyse_th45d.py` (s3_scored.csv). Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this. **1 script needs the internet**, which is off during the run: wikidata_p39_531.py. info.title: Does Numerology Foretell a Life? Preregistered Tests on Legislators, Olympians and Laureates, and a Lesson on Identity Leakage When Language Models Judge Blind

text.text: Numerology, sun-sign astrology and the Japanese system sanmeigaku claim that the date of birth (and, for numerology, the name) shows whether a person will rise and when their life will turn.

We tested 33 such predictions (excluding the blind matching test described below), preregistered on the Open Science Framework, on four populations with third-party records: 3,308 members of the Japanese House of Representatives, 120,798 national legislators worldwide, 156,386 Olympic athletes, and 8,296 nominees for the Nobel Prize or an Academy Award and Japanese Persons of Cultural Merit.
None was supported.

Leadership numbers and signs did not predict becoming a leader, an Olympic champion or a laureate, and beginnings, endings and deaths did not cluster in the predicted years; in the largest samples, several differences from chance lay within preregistered bounds of practical equivalence.

A positive control, the relative-age effect among Olympic football and ice-hockey players, was detected with the same data and methods (30.0% born January-March against 24.7% of days; p = 1.8 × 10 ²⁴).
In a preregistered blind ⁻ matching test, one language model wrote a numerology reading and a model from another provider picked the person's life summary out of five.
When the reading model was given names, the judge matched readings to summaries well above chance, largely because the reading model wrote the names into the readings against its instructions.
Given only the numbers, the judge matched at chance worldwide (20.4%) but at 28.0% in Japan.
A follow-up, registered after the first submission, asked the judge to identify each person from the summary alone.

In trials in which the judge had not identified the target by both name and exact date of birth, hit rates were 18.5% worldwide and 25.5% in Japan (95% CI 19.0-32.8%), and the judge chose summaries whose recalled birth dates reproduced the reading's numbers more often than chance.
The systems did not foretell lives.
A language model asked to judge readings blind can appear to succeed by recognising the person, and instructions alone do not prevent this.

Numerology, astrology and the East Asian calendar arts share one claim: a fixed property of a person's birth (the date, sometimes the hour, and for numerology the letters of the name) indicates the kind of life the person will lead and the timing of its turning points.
Practitioners support the claim with single striking cases.

For example, by the numerological rules used in this paper, 2022, the year in which former Prime Minister Abe Shinzo of Japan was assassinated, was his "Personal Year 9", the year of endings (born 21 September 1954: 9 + 3 +6 = 18 → 9).
The author computed this case by hand while drafting the first registration, which discloses it.
A single case cannot test such a claim.
Any outcome can be matched to some meaning after the fact, and the people with the same numbers to whom nothing happened are not counted.

This paper tests the claims on whole populations whose careers and lives are recorded by third parties: members of the Japanese House of Representatives since 1947, national legislators worldwide, Olympic athletes, and nominees for major science and arts honours.
Before any number was computed for a population, the rules of each system, the outcomes and the tests were fixed in a preregistration (Registrations 1-4; Section 5.6 gives the order of events).
We test three systems: • Pythagorean numerology derives a Life Path number from the date of birth, an Expression number from the name, and a Personal Year number for each calendar year.
It describes 1, 8 and 22 as numbers of leadership, Personal Year 1 as a year of beginnings and Personal Year 9 as a year of endings.
• Sun-sign astrology associates Aries, Leo and Capricorn with leadership, Jupiter's passage through the natal sun sign with expansion and success, and Saturn's passage with trial and endings.

• Sanmeigaku, a Japanese system built on the Chinese sexagenary calendar, assigns each person two "void" years in every twelve (tenchusatsu) from the day of birth, and teaches that what is begun in those years does not last and that they bring endings.
The study also includes a modern version of Carlson's (1985) double-blind test of astrology, in which language models replace the astrologers.
text.formatted: The study also includes a modern version of <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Carlson's (1985)</ref> double-blind test of astrology, in which language models replace the astrologers.

text.text: Its result proved the most informative part of the study, for reasons that bear more on research with language models than on numerology.
A model asked to judge a reading blind can recognise the person behind the material and use what it knows about that person.
We tested this route directly in a preregistered follow-up (Section 6.6).
The systems did not arise from records of people's lives, and their history explains both why they take the form they do and why they persist.
Three points are documented.
First, the calendar arts began as tools of the state, not of the individual.
Mesopotamian celestial omens concerned almost entirely the king, the army and the country (Rochberg, 2004).
text.formatted: Mesopotamian celestial omens concerned almost entirely the king, the army and the country <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Rochberg, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The earliest known horoscopes cast for individuals date from 410 BCE in Babylonia, and only a few dozen cuneiform horoscopes survive; Greek manuals for casting them appear from the late second century BCE (Rochberg, 1998).
text.formatted: The earliest known horoscopes cast for individuals date from 410 BCE in Babylonia, and only a few dozen cuneiform horoscopes survive; Greek manuals for casting them appear from the late second century BCE <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Rochberg, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: The Chinese sexagenary cycle on which sanmeigaku rests was first a way of counting days: in the oracle-bone inscriptions of the Shang it dates divinations (Boltz, 2019).
text.formatted: The Chinese sexagenary cycle on which sanmeigaku rests was first a way of counting days: in the oracle-bone inscriptions of the Shang it dates divinations <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Boltz, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Reading a person's fate from the stems and branches of the birth date is usually traced to the Tang and Song dynasties (Ho, 2003).
text.formatted: Reading a person's fate from the stems and branches of the birth date is usually traced to the Tang and Song dynasties <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ho, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Each system thus applies to the individual an instrument made for calendars and states.
Second, the material is the date of birth and the name because every person has them, nobody chooses them, and they can be turned into numbers.
A fixed computation always gives an answer, and a fixed procedure looks objective.
Practitioners therefore often describe these systems as "statistics" (Section 2), although none of them was built by counting outcomes.
Third, the modern forms that circulate today are recent.

The numerology of Life Path and Expression numbers was largely created in the early twentieth century in the United States, with Mrs L. Dow Balliett as its main early author; there is no evidence that the Pythagoreans divined in this way (Dudley, 1997; Genovese, 2017).
text.formatted: The numerology of Life Path and Expression numbers was largely created in the early twentieth century in the United States, with Mrs L. Dow Balliett as its main early author; there is no evidence that the Pythagoreans divined in this way <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dudley, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Genovese, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In Japan, stroke-count name divination in its now dominant form was published by Kumazaki Ken'ō in 1929, in a book from Jitsugyō no Nihon-sha and in the women's magazine Shufu no Tomo (Kumazaki, 1929; National Diet Library catalogue).
text.formatted: In Japan, stroke-count name divination in its now dominant form was published by Kumazaki Ken'ō in 1929, in a book from Jitsugyō no Nihon-sha and in the women's magazine Shufu no Tomo <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kumazaki, 1929;</ref> <ref type="bibr">National Diet Library catalogue)</ref>.

text.text: By 1932 a rival author was publicly accusing him of lying (Nemoto, 1932).
text.formatted: By 1932 a rival author was publicly accusing him of lying <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Nemoto, 1932)</ref>.

text.text: Tenchusatsu is a renaming of the Four Pillars concept of kongwang ("emptiness"); it reached a mass public in the late 1970s, when a sanmeigaku practitioner predicted on television that the Yomiuri Giants would not win the Japan Series, and his introductory books became best-sellers (Izumi, 1979).
text.formatted: Tenchusatsu is a renaming of the Four Pillars concept of kongwang ("emptiness"); it reached a mass public in the late 1970s, when a sanmeigaku practitioner predicted on television that the Yomiuri Giants would not win the Japan Series, and his introductory books became best-sellers <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Izumi, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Each modern form spread through mass print and broadcast media.
We suggest, as an interpretation rather than a documented finding, that this demand grew as individuals, rather than families or villages, increasingly made choices about marriage, work and names.
Section 7.2 returns to why the systems persist when, as this paper shows, they do not predict.
Numerology.
Despite its popularity, numerology has, as far as we could find, one peer-reviewed empirical test.
Genovese (2017) computed one birth number for 806 Nobel laureates and found no departure from a uniform distribution (χ²(8) = 4.92, p = .77) and no association with prize category.

Related archival work on "birthday numbers" (Pelham et al., 2002) was later traced to cohort, geographic and ethnic confounds (Simonsohn, 2011). Phillips et al. (2001) reported more cardiac deaths among Chinese and Japanese Americans on the 4th of the month, a number associated with death; the effect depended on the choice of diagnostic codes (Smith, 2002) and did not appear in Hong Kong (Panesar et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Related archival work on "birthday numbers" <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Pelham et al., 2002)</ref> was later traced to cohort, geographic and ethnic confounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Simonsohn, 2011)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Phillips et al. (2001)</ref> reported more cardiac deaths among Chinese and Japanese Americans on the 4th of the month, a number associated with death; the effect depended on the choice of diagnostic codes <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Smith, 2002)</ref> and did not appear in Hong Kong <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Panesar et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: No study has tested Life Path, Expression or Personal Year numbers against life outcomes.
Astrology.
Astrology has been tested often.

In Carlson's (1985) double-blind test, astrologers matched natal charts to the right one of three personality profiles in 40 of 116 cases, against 38.5 expected by chance and 58.5 predicted by the astrologers.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Carlson's (1985)</ref> double-blind test, astrologers matched natal charts to the right one of three personality profiles in 40 of 116 cases, against 38.5 expected by chance and 58.5 predicted by the astrologers.

text.text: Students could not pick their own computer-generated natalchart reading out of two (Wyman & Vyse, 2008).
text.formatted: Students could not pick their own computer-generated natalchart reading out of two <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Wyman & Vyse, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: People born minutes apart in London in 1958 were no more alike than chance on 110 variables (Dean & Kelly, 2003).
text.formatted: People born minutes apart in London in 1958 were no more alike than chance on 110 variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Dean & Kelly, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Large samples found no relation between sun signs and personality or intelligence: about 15,000 in Hartmann et al. (2006), 65,268 in Steyn (2011) and about 173,000 in Lu et al. (2020).
text.formatted: Large samples found no relation between sun signs and personality or intelligence: about 15,000 in <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hartmann et al. (2006)</ref>, 65,268 in <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Steyn (2011)</ref> and about 173,000 in <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lu et al. (2020)</ref>.

text.text: Swedish registers showed no relation between sign compatibility and marriage or divorce (Helgertz & Scott, 2020).
text.formatted: Swedish registers showed no relation between sign compatibility and marriage or divorce <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Helgertz & Scott, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A review of about a thousand studies concludes that sun signs are the most tested and most disconfirmed idea in astrology (Dean et al., 2022).
text.formatted: A review of about a thousand studies concludes that sun signs are the most tested and most disconfirmed idea in astrology <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Dean et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The Mars-effect controversy showed how selection of cases by an interested party can create an effect (Nienhuys, 1997).
text.formatted: The Mars-effect controversy showed how selection of cases by an interested party can create an effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Nienhuys, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: We found no peer-reviewed study of politicians' or athletes' sun signs that we could verify, and no study relating planetary transits to careers.
We found no empirical test of sanmeigaku or tenchusatsu.
Searches of J-STAGE and CiNii Research (24 October 2026) for 算命学, 天中殺, 四柱推命 and 数秘術 returned practitioner books and magazines, historical and literary studies, and no test.
The related Korean Four Pillars system has one small correlational study (n = 148; Jung & Yang, 2015), with weak correlations and no correction for multiple tests.
text.formatted: The related Korean Four Pillars system has one small correlational study (n = 148; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Jung & Yang, 2015)</ref>, with weak correlations and no correction for multiple tests.

text.text: Two features of birth dates can create spurious "effects" of birth-based systems.
First, relative age: children who are the oldest in their school year or sports cohort do better, and selection reflects this.
Leading members of the US Congress were more often the oldest in their cohort (Muller & Page, 2016).
text.formatted: Leading members of the US Congress were more often the oldest in their cohort <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Muller & Page, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Being born on 1 January rather than 31 December raised Finnish male candidates' chance of election by 6.9 percentage points (Tukiainen et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Being born on 1 January rather than 31 December raised Finnish male candidates' chance of election by 6.9 percentage points <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Tukiainen et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Belgian MPs born just after the cutoff were over-represented by up to 90% (Al Yussef et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Belgian MPs born just after the cutoff were over-represented by up to 90% <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Al Yussef et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In sports whose youth categories are defined by calendar year, players born early in the year are over-represented (Cobley et al., 2009).
text.formatted: In sports whose youth categories are defined by calendar year, players born early in the year are over-represented <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Cobley et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Japan's school year starts on 2 April, so people born from 1 January to 1 April are the youngest in their year (Kawaguchi, 2011; Uemura, 2019).
text.formatted: Japan's school year starts on 2 April, so people born from 1 January to 1 April are the youngest in their year <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kawaguchi, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Uemura, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These dates overlap Capricorn and the start of Aries.
Second, recorded birth dates heap on round days, especially in older records (Lledó et al., 2025; Nguyen, 2017).
text.formatted: Second, recorded birth dates heap on round days, especially in older records <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Lledó et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Nguyen, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Calendar beliefs themselves alter records: girls born in the 1966 fire-horse year were registered under other years (Grech, 2016).
text.formatted: Calendar beliefs themselves alter records: girls born in the 1966 fire-horse year were registered under other years <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Grech, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Wikidata birth dates disagree between sources in about 2% of cases (Laouenan et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Wikidata birth dates disagree between sources in about 2% of cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Laouenan et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The tests below control for birth-date structure by permutation within strata, and report sensitivity analyses that remove heaped dates.
Beliefs that act.
Calendar beliefs have measurable effects even when their predictions fail.
Births in Japan fell by about 463,000 in the fire-horse year 1966 (Kaku, 1975; Rohlfs et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Births in Japan fell by about 463,000 in the fire-horse year 1966 <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kaku, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Rohlfs et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Dragon-year births rise in Chinese populations (Yip et al., 2002), and dragon-year children do better at school because of parents' expectations (Mocan & Yu, 2020).
text.formatted: Dragon-year births rise in Chinese populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Yip et al., 2002)</ref>, and dragon-year children do better at school because of parents' expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Mocan & Yu, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Applicants with a Virgo birthday were less likely to be hired in China (Lu et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Applicants with a Virgo birthday were less likely to be hired in China <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Lu et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Whether the systems predict is therefore a separate question from whether people act on them.
Language models as readers and judges.
Users already consult large language models for Four Pillars and other readings (Lin et al., 2026), and belief in AI predictions correlates with belief in astrology (Lee et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Users already consult large language models for Four Pillars and other readings <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Lin et al., 2026)</ref>, and belief in AI predictions correlates with belief in astrology <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Lee et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Language models are also increasingly used as judges of text in research.

A model that has seen a person's biography in training can recognise the person from indirect cues; in evaluation research, the analogous problem of test material that the model has already seen is known as data contamination (Sainz et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A model that has seen a person's biography in training can recognise the person from indirect cues; in evaluation research, the analogous problem of test material that the model has already seen is known as data contamination <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Sainz et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We found no study in which a language model writes a reading and a different model then matches it blind, and no study that tests whether such a judge recognises the persons.
Contribution.
This is the first preregistered test of numerology, sun-sign astrology and sanmeigaku against careers, honours and deaths, on four populations and with a positive control.
It documents the practitioner sources of each tested rule, and it reports a preregistered test of identity recall by a languagemodel judge.
The rules were taken from widely circulated practitioner sources rather than from one author, and the registrations fixed one version of each before the data were compiled.
Practitioners disagree on several details.

Table 1 lists the sources and the disagreements, and the last column reports, as an exploratory check run after the confirmatory results were known, the Study 3 and 4 results under each variant that could be computed from the data already collected (source_variants.py).

Data The paper reports four preregistered studies.
Study 1 and the companion astrology and sanmeigaku test (Part 1) use members of the Japanese House of Representatives.
Study 2 and the companion test (Part 2) use national legislators worldwide.
Studies 3 and 4 use Olympic athletes and award nominees and test numerology, astrology and sanmeigaku together.
All registrations are in one OSF project (Registration 1, Study 1; Registration 2, Study 2; Registration 3, astrology and sanmeigaku for Studies 1 and 2; Registration 4, Studies 3 and 4).
Population.
Every person elected to the House of Representatives at a general election from 1947 to 2024, plus members who entered the House at a by-election in that period.
Winners were compiled from the Japanese Wikipedia result tables of each general election and by-election, retrieved on 24 October 2026.

Dates of birth, names in kanji and kana readings were taken from Wikidata and, where Wikidata lacked them, from the lead section of the member's Japanese Wikipedia article (365 dates of birth and 124 readings).
The kana reading was romanised in Hepburn without macrons (family name first) by a fixed script.
Where the birth name differed from the name at first election and the birth name was known, the birth name was used, as registered.
The final population is 3,308 members with a full date of birth.
Outcomes.
• Prime Minister and cabinet member.

The lists of cabinets published by the Prime Minister's Office (Kantei) were matched to members by name, with normalised character variants, a fixed alias table for three names, and matching by reading for 61 names with rare characters.
Study 1 used the lists up to retrieval (October 2026: 37 Prime Ministers, 722 cabinet members).
Part 1 used the registered cut-off of the end of 2024 (36 and 705).
• First election.
Study 1 uses the year of first election from 1947 onward (2,883 members for H3a).

Part 1 uses the day of first election and goes back to the Imperial Diet where winner lists exist; 33 members first elected in 1894-1904, for which Wikipedia has no complete winner tables, could not be dated to the day and are excluded from A2 and S2.
• End of service.
The end of the member's last term in the House and its reason (defeat or retirement at the next general election, death, resignation, loss of seat or expiry of term).
Study 1 uses the year; Part 1 uses the day, with the registered cut-off of 31 December 2024.
• Correction of the members coded as in office.
The original compilation coded 531 members as still in office on 31 December 2024 and excluded them from the end-of-service tests.
The House has 465 seats.
After the first submission, the 531 were checked against the 465 winners of the 50th general election of 27 October 2024 (Japanese Wikipedia, revision 111562417, retrieved 11 November 2026).
All 465 winners were among the 531, and no resignation or death between the election and 31 December 2024 was found.

The other 66 had not won the 50th election: 51 were in office at the dissolution of 9 October 2024 (49 defeated, 2 retired), and 15 had left the House earlier (between 2000 and 2021) and returned only at the 51st election of 2026.
text.formatted: The other 66 had not won the 50th election: 51 were in office at the dissolution of 9 October 2024 (49 defeated, 2 retired), and 15 had left the House earlier <ref type="bibr">(between 2000 and 2021)</ref> and returned only at the 51st election of 2026.

text.text: The compilation had treated every winner of the 2026 election as serving.
Under the registered definition of Part 1 (the last day of the final continuous spell ending on or before 31 December 2024), the 66 receive that end date.
For Part 1 the original coding was therefore an error.

Registration 1 sets no cut-off date for Study 1, so its original coding, which counted only completed final spells at the time of compilation, is defensible; we report it as registered and add two corrected versions.

The main corrected version applies the 31 December 2024 status to all 531 members: the 66 receive their end year, and the 173 winners of the 50th election whose service ended in 2025 or 2026 lose those end years, because they were in office on 31 December 2024 (H3b: n = 2,843 instead of 2,950).
A second version changes only the 66 (n = 3,016).
Section 6.1 reports all three.
Population.

Every person in Wikidata with a "position held" (P39) whose position is a direct subclass of "member of parliament" (Q486839), with a day-precision date of birth on or after 1 January 1800 (snapshot of 24 October 2026).
Of 169,108 legislators with any birth record, 40,560 lacked a dayprecision date of birth, 6,571 were born before 1800 and 1,179 had conflicting birth dates; 120,798 are in scope.
Country is the country of the legislature seat (P17 or P1001), or, where missing, the country of citizenship (P27); 204 persons had no country.
Names.
The birth name (P1477) where recorded in Latin script, otherwise the English Wikidata label; 10,635 persons have neither and are excluded from the Expression test.
Outcomes.

Head of state or head of government: a position held that is the value of P1906 or P1313 of an item that is an instance of "country" (Q6256); 1,402 legislators held such an office, 1,385 with a recorded start date.
The leadership tests use the 111,447 legislators of the 160 countries in which at least one legislator, but not all, held such an office (1,398 office holders).
Date of death: P570; 62,914 deceased persons have a year of death and a country.
Population.

Every athlete with an Olympedia identifier (Wikidata P8286) and a single day-precision date of birth from 1800 onward who competed at the Summer or Winter Olympic Games from 1896 to 2024: 156,386 athletes, of whom 3,679 with conflicting birth dates were excluded beforehand.
Outcome.
At least one Olympic gold medal, from the Olympedia medal tables of each Games (11,314 gold medallists).
The registered date of the first gold medal is the date of the final of the event, with the opening date of the Games as the flagged fallback.
Event dates were not retrieved, so the opening date was used for all gold medals (a deviation).
Covariates.
National Olympic Committee, sport, sex and birth decade.
As a deviation (Section 5.7), country and sport were taken from Wikidata rather than from each athlete's Olympedia page.
Positive control.

Among Olympic football and ice-hockey players born in 1970 or later (7,252 players), two sports whose international youth categories are defined by calendar year of birth, the registered prediction was an over-representation of births in January to March relative to their share of calendar days.

Three pools from Wikidata (snapshot after registration): persons nominated for a Nobel Prize (pool N; 2,250 with a single day-precision date of birth from 1800; 385 laureates), persons nominated for an Academy Award (pool A; 5,187; 1,762 winners), and Japanese Persons of Cultural Merit or recipients of the Order of Culture (pool J; 859; 425 recipients of the Order of Culture).
The outcome is winning within the pool.
The date of the first win is 10 December of the award year (Nobel), the ceremony date (Academy Award) and 3 November of the year (Order of Culture), as registered.
Names follow the Study 2 rules.
Study 1 sample.

Members who had died by 31 December 2024 and whose service had ended were shuffled with seed 20261024 and taken in that order, skipping those whose Japanese Wikipedia text had fewer than 400 characters, until 200 members had a life summary that passed the screening in Section 5.4.
Deceased legislators with a day-precision date of death who never held head-of-state or head-of-government office, whose Wikidata item has fewer than 10 sitelinks, and who have a Latin-script name.

After shuffling with the same seed, the first 500 persons with at least four other eligible persons of the same country and birth decade were taken as targets; 2,447 persons appear as target or decoy.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="5." >Methods</head>

text.text: Pythagorean letter values: A J S = 1; B K T = 2; C L U = 3; D M V = 4; E N W = 5; F O X = 6; G P Y = 7; H Q Z = 8; I R = 9.
• Life Path: the digits of the full date of birth are summed and reduced by repeated digit summing to 1-9, keeping the master numbers 11, 22 and 33.
• Expression: the letter values of the full name are summed and reduced in the same way, keeping 11, 22 and 33.
Diacritics are removed.
• Personal Year for calendar year Y: the digits of the birth month and day plus the digits of Y, reduced to 1-9 without master numbers.
The registered check case (born 21 September 1954, year 2022) gives Personal Year 9.
• Leadership numbers: 1, 8 and 22.
• Ephemeris.
JPL DE440, as registered (Park et al., 2021), via Skyfield (Rhodes, 2019).
text.formatted: JPL DE440, as registered <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Park et al., 2021)</ref>, via Skyfield <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Rhodes, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For Studies 1 and 2 the file came from the Python package naif-de440, whose MD5 checksum equals the one NAIF publishes for de440.bsp.
The registered validation script ran with zero failures.
The registered calculation script was placed in the project six minutes after Registration 3 was submitted (Section 5.6).

For Studies 3 and 4 the confirmatory run used astronomy-engine (VSOP87) because DE440 could not be retrieved in the computing environment at the time (a deviation); a later recomputation with DE440 changed one sun sign among 8,296 persons in Study 4 and one boundary-day flag among 156,386 in Study 3, and no event-date value.
• Sun sign.
The apparent geocentric ecliptic longitude of the Sun (of date) at 12:00 Japan time (Part 1) or 12:00 UTC (all other tests) on the date of birth.
Persons born on a day on which the Sun changes sign are flagged and excluded in a sensitivity analysis.
• Transits.
Jupiter or Saturn is "in the sun sign" when its longitude at noon on the event date lies in the same 30-degree sign as the natal Sun.
• Sanmeigaku.
The day pillar of the birth date (sexagenary cycle anchored at 1 January2000 = 戊 午) gives the two void branches (tenchusatsu) of the person's ten-day group.
A year is a tenchusatsu year when its earthly branch is one of the two; the branch of a year changes at risshun (Sun at 315 degrees).
• Confidence intervals for timing tests (added after the first submission).
For the observed share we report a Wilson 95% interval.
For the difference between the observed share and the permutation mean we report the interval [observed -97.5th percentile, observed -2.5th percentile] of the permutation distribution.

This is the null band of the permutation distribution shifted to the observed share; it is an approximate interval that assumes a departure from chance would shift the distribution without changing its shape.
With the original scripts and seeds, the reproduced n, observed share, permutation mean and p agree exactly with the confirmatory output for all reproduced tests.
• Multiple testing and equivalence.
Holm correction within each registered family: seven tests in Study 1, five in Study 2, six in Part 1, five in Part 2, and six in each of Studies 3 and 4.
Equivalence bounds, where registered: odds ratios between 0.90 and 1.11, and differences of less than 1 percentage point from the permutation mean (TOST).

The bounds were chosen as effects too small to matter to anyone consulting these systems: on base rates of 8-17%, one percentage point is a relative change of 6-12%, and an odds ratio of 1.11 is far below the strong associations the systems claim.
Registration 3 does not claim equivalence from non-significance; it relies on confidence intervals.
The design follows Carlson (1985).
text.formatted: The design follows <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Carlson (1985)</ref>.

text.text: A language model writes a numerology reading.
A model from a different provider receives the reading and five anonymous life summaries, one of which belongs to the person, and chooses one.
The chance hit rate is 1/5.
• Models.
Readings and Study 1 summaries: Anthropic claude-sonnet-5-5.
Judge: OpenAI gpt-6sol (Responses API).
Default sampling settings.
The model strings returned by the APIs were logged with every call.
• Life summaries.

Study 1: an English summary of about 120 words written from the Japanese Wikipedia text, with personal names, place names, dates, party names and names of posts removed; a script rejected any summary containing a digit or any part of the member's name.
Study 2: built by a fixed script from Wikidata facts only (positions held, party, occupations and age at death).
• Decoys.
Study 1: four other members of the sample drawn at random.
Study 2: four persons of the same country and birth decade.
The order of the five summaries was randomised (seed 20261024).
• First run (H4, as registered).
The reading model received the romanised name and the date of birth, with the instruction to write a reading of about 150 words and not to name or allude to any real person.
• Numbers-only run (H4-N).
Registered after the first run and before any H4-N output existed.

The reading model receives only the numbers that numerology derives from the name and date of birth: Life Path, Expression, Soul Urge, Personality, Birthday number and the four Pinnacles with their age ranges.
Persons, summaries, decoys, orders, judge and judge instruction are identical to the first run.
• Tests.
One-sided exact binomial test of the hit rate against 0.20 in each study; for H4-N, an exact McNemar test against the first run on the same trials.
The reading model in H4-N received the Life Path and Birthday numbers, both functions of the date of birth.
A judge that recognises a person from the life summary and recalls the person's date of birth could compare it with the numbers in the reading.
This route was not addressed by the original registrations.

After the first submission, the author ran informal exploratory probes of identity leakage (25-26 October 2026; scripts, caches and a findings note are in the project; they used other prompts and are not reported here).
A journal editor then asked for a formal test.
The check below was registered as an update to Registrations 1 and 2 on 11 November 2026, approved before any output of the registered check existed, and is reported as an exploratory deviation.
• Procedure.

Every distinct summary that appeared in an H4-N trial (200 Study 1 persons; 2,447 Study 2 persons, 2,395 distinct texts because some template summaries coincide) was sent alone to the registered judge with the prompt: "Here is a short summary of a real person's career.
Who is this person?
Reply only with JSON: {"name": string or null, "date_of_birth": "YYYY-MM-DD" or null, "confidence": integer 0-100}.
If you do not know, use null."
One call per distinct summary, cached; an invalid reply would be retried once.
• Scoring.
Name identified: the reply matches the registered name after removing diacritics and case (family name and at least one given name; Study 1, the kanji name or its registered Hepburn romanisation).
Date of birth recalled: exact match.
• Analyses.

A1: H4-N hit rate in trials whose target was identified with the correct date of birth, and in all other trials; exact one-sided binomial test of the second group against 0.20; Fisher's exact test between groups.

A2: for each trial and each of the five summaries, the numbers the reading model would have received if the judge's recalled date (not the true date) were used; summaries whose implied numbers equal those given to the reading model are "marked"; the share of trials in which the judge chose a marked summary is compared with the share expected if the judge chose at random among the five (exact Poisson-binomial test).
A3 (Study 2): logistic regression of the H4-N hit on log(1 + sitelinks), with and without the identification indicator.
• Registered reading.

If the hit rate in trials without identification is not above 0.20 and the judge's choices concentrate on marked summaries, the H4-N result is attributed to identity recall; if hits above 0.20 remain in trials without identification, identity recall does not explain the result and its source is unidentified.

text.text: Other disclosures.

Before the confirmatory run of Registration 3, the analysis code was checked on data with shuffled outcomes but unshuffled event dates, so its eight timing tests were in effect computed on the real data at that stage; the confirmatory run, made once with the same seed, gave identical values.
Study 1 counted cabinet posts up to October 2026 because its registration set no end date; it is also reported with end-2024 lists.

After the first submission and before the registered identity-recall check, informal exploratory probes of identity leakage were run (25-26 October 2026); their scripts and outputs are in the project and they are not used in this paper.
Analyses labelled exploratory were added after the confirmatory runs.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="6." >Results</head>

text.text: Members with a leadership Life Path number made up 29.7% of the 37 Prime Ministers and 26.0% of the other members (H1a: odds ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.57-2.37, p = 0.68; Fisher's exact p = 0.58), and 28.1% of the 722 cabinet members against 25.5% of other members (H1b: 1.11, 0.92-1.34, p = 0.29).
Results for the Expression number were similar (H2a: 1.49, 0.73-3.05, p = 0.27; H2b: 0.98, 0.80-1.21, p = 0.88).
First elections fell in Personal Year 1 for 11.17% of 2,883 members, against 11.20% under permutation (H3a: difference -0.03 percentage points, 95% CI -0.31 to +0.24; p = 0.90).
Ends of service fell in Personal Year 9 for 10.75% of 2,950 members, against 11.07% (H3b: -0.33, -1.39 to +0.71; p = 0.55).

After correcting the 66 members wrongly coded as in office (Section 4.1), the share was 10.69% of 2,843 members against 11.06% (-0.36, -1.44 to +0.70; p = 0.51); with only the 66 changed and all other end years as originally coded, 10.71% of 3,016 against 10.98% (p = 0.63).
After Holm correction across the seven registered tests, each of the six has p = 1.00.

Excluding members whose birth name was not known (H2a: 1.68, 0.81-3.47; H2b: 1.00, 0.81-1.22), cutting the cabinet lists at the end of 2024, and removing 73 members born on 1 January or 1 to 3 April (all p ≥ 0.22) did not change the results; every confidence interval includes 1.

Among 111,447 legislators in the 160 countries with variation in the outcome, the 1,398 heads of state or government were not more likely to have a leadership Life Path number (24.5% against 26.1%; H1: OR 0.90, 0.79-1.03, p = 0.13) or Expression number (20.5% against 22.3%; H2: 0.88, 0.76-1.01, p = 0.064).
Both estimates point opposite to the prediction; the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios stratified by country (0.93 and 0.88) agree.
Of 1,385 leaders with a recorded start date, 11.91% took office in Personal Year 1, against 11.36% expected (H3a: +0.55 pp, -0.65 to +1.73; p = 0.39).

Of 62,914 deceased legislators, 11.27% died in Personal Year 9, against 11.11% expected (H3b: +0.16 pp, -0.08 to +0.41; p = 0.20); the difference lies within the preregistered ±1-point equivalence margin (TOST p = 6.7 × 10 ¹²).
Holm-⁻ adjusted p-values: 0.39, 0.25, 0.39 and 0.39.
Checks without Japan, with birth-month dummies, and without the 1,256 legislators born on 1 January gave the same results.
None of the eleven registered tests supported the prediction (Table 5).

text.text: Aries, Leo and Capricorn made up 27.8% of the 36 Prime Ministers to the end of 2024 and 26.2% of other members (A1a: OR 1.16, 0.55-2.43; Fisher's p = 0.85); the odds ratio for the 705 cabinet members was 0.99 and worldwide for heads of state or government 1.05 (0.92-1.19).
Jupiter in the sun sign, Saturn in the sun sign and tenchusatsu years showed no excess at first elections, ends of service, accessions or deaths.
After the correction of Section 4.1, A3 and S1 in Japan gave 7.90% against 8.37% (p = 0.34) and 16.27% against 16.85% (p = 0.38).
The registered sensitivity analyses did not change these results.
One unadjusted p-value fell below 0.05: worldwide without Japan, Saturn was in the sun sign at slightly fewer deaths than expected (p = 0.041), opposite to the prediction.

text.text: Among 156,386 Olympians, the odds of a gold medal did not differ by leadership Life Path number (OR 0.99, 0.95-1.04), Expression number (1.00, 0.95-1.05; 154,781 athletes with a name) or sign (1.00, 0.95-1.05); all three lie within the registered equivalence bounds.
First gold medals did not cluster in Personal Year 1, in Jupiter years or outside tenchusatsu years; all three differences lie within ±1 percentage point (equivalence shown).
Among 8,296 nominees and honourees, the odds of winning were 1.01 (0.91-1.13), 1.00 (0.89-1.12; 8,244 with a name) and 0.99 (0.89-1.11), and the first wins did not cluster in the predicted years.

With 2,572 winners, equivalence could be shown for only two of the six tests, and narrowly (P-N2, TOST p = 0.041; P-A1, p = 0.046); without births on 1 January, P-A1 just misses the equivalence criterion (TOST p = 0.052).
Birthmonth dummies and the exclusion of births on 1 January did not change the estimates.
The positive control was detected.

Of 7,252 Olympic football and ice-hockey players born in 1970 or later, 30.0% were born in January to March, against 24.7% of calendar days (one-sided p = 1.8 × 10 ²⁴); ⁻ the quarterly shares fell from 30.0% to 26.5%, 23.4% and 20.1%.
The same data found the relative-age effect, a real effect of the birth date produced by the way youth sport selects players.
The positive control is a test of the birth-date distribution and does not exercise the regressions or permutation tests themselves; their sensitivity is shown by their confidence intervals.
In Study 3, odds ratios above 1.05 for the success groups and timing differences larger than about 0.9 percentage points lie outside the 95% intervals.

Under the variants of Table 1 (Decoz's reduction of the Life Path, a birthday-start Personal Year, cardinal or Scorpio-inclusive leadership signs), Studies 3 and 4 gave the same results: odds ratios between 0.95 and 1.03 and timing differences within 0.6 percentage points (exploratory).

text.text: First run, as registered (H4).
The judge picked the true summary in 146 of 200 trials in Japan (73.0%; p = 1.7 × 10 ⁵⁸) and in 277 of 500 worldwide (55.4%; p = 4.7 × 10 ⁶⁸), against 20% by chance.
By the ⁻ ⁻ registered criterion, H4 is supported in both studies.

The reading model, however, had written the person's name into 162 of the 200 readings in Japan and 401 of the 500 worldwide, against its instruction, typically as a heading ("Numerology Reading: [name]").
The registration of Study 2 states that the judge does not see names; this condition was not met.
Fifty-eight readings were empty (11 in Japan, 47 worldwide).
Worldwide, readings that named the person hit 61.8% of the time, readings that did not name the person 28.8% (15 of 52), and empty readings 29.8% (14 of 47).
In Japan, readings that did not name the person still hit 63.0% (17 of 27), consistent with the reading model shaping readings to the known careers of members it recognised.
With only the numbers, no reading named the person.
Worldwide the judge picked the true summary in 102 of 500 trials (20.4%; p = 0.43; also significantly below the registered equivalence bound of 25%, p = 0.009).
In Japan it picked it in 56 of 200 (28.0%; one-sided p = 0.004).
Compared trial by trial with the first run, 96 trials in Japan and 191 worldwide were hits only in the first run, against 6 and 16 only in H4-N (McNemar p = 5.7 × 10 ²² and 3.2 × 10 ³⁹).
Identity-recall check.
Given each summary alone, the judge named 63 of the 200 Study 1 targets correctly (31.5%) and gave the exact date of birth for 36 (18.0%); 35 (17.5%) were identified by both.
Worldwide, it named 60 of the 500 targets (12.0%), gave the exact date of birth for 38 (7.6%), and identified 36 (7.2%) by both.

Hit-rate intervals are exact (Clopper-Pearson).
A "marked" summary is one whose date of birth, as recalled by the judge, reproduces the numbers given to the reading model in that trial.

The run stopped after 1,838 of 2,595 summaries when the API account ran out of credit; after credit was added, the remaining 757 summaries were called from the cache (no summary was called twice), and all analyses use all trials.
Estimated cost: USD 24.66.
Worldwide, the overall H4-N hit rate was already at chance (20.4%), so the question is what drives the hits that do occur and the sitelinks gradient.

In the 464 trials whose target the judge did not identify, the hit rate was 18.5%, at chance, while it was 44.4% when it did; and the judge chose summaries whose recalled birth dates reproduced the reading's numbers far more often than at random.
By the registered reading, the worldwide hits are attributed to identity recall.
The sitelinks gradient, however, remains after the identification indicator is added (OR 2.48), and the indicator itself is not significant in that model (p = 0.088).

The gradient is consistent with partial recognition that falls short of the exact name and date and with the judge's preference for longer summaries, which belong to more prominent persons (45.6% of H4-N choices were the longest summary, against 20%; results/supplementary.json).
Identity recall does not explain it alone.

In Japan both registered conditions hold: in the 165 trials without identification the hit rate (25.5%) was not shown to be above 0.20 (p = 0.052), and the judge chose marked summaries twice as often as at random (7.0% against 3.6%; p = 0.007).
By the registered reading, the Japanese H4-N result is therefore attributed to identity recall.
We add a caution that goes beyond the registered rule.
Of the 16 hits above chance (56 against 40 expected), about 7 come from the 35 identified trials (14 against 7 expected) and about 9 from the other 165 (42 against 33).
The interval for the latter (19.0-32.8%) does not exclude an excess of that size.

In an unregistered secondary analysis that counts identification by the date of birth alone (one member was answered with the exact date under a different romanisation of his name), the rate in unidentified trials is 25.6% (p = 0.048).
Part of the Japanese excess may therefore have other sources, such as era and sex cues carried by Japanese given names in decoy sets not matched on era or sex (exploratory analyses in the project).
>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="7." >Discussion</head>

text.text: Across 33 registered tests of numerology, sun-sign astrology and sanmeigaku on four populations, none was supported, and several estimates pointed opposite to the prediction.

The largest tests had more than 100,000 persons and thousands of events; in them the odds ratios lay between 0.88 and 1.05, and the differences of timing tests from chance within about half a percentage point.
Equivalence was shown for Personal Year 9 at death among 62,914 legislators and for all six tests among 156,386 Olympians.
The Japanese Prime Minister tests, with 36 or 37 events, cannot rule out large effects; the evidence on leadership comes mainly from the cabinet, worldwide, Olympic and laureate tests.
The positive control shows that the null results are not the product of an insensitive design: the same data and methods detected the relative-age effect at p = 1.8 × 10 ²⁴.
The practitioner variants of the rules gave the same ⁻ results, so the null results do not depend on choosing one school's version.
The results do not test why the systems persist; the following four reasons are our interpretation, supported by the history in Section 1.1 and by the studies cited.
First, the systems serve purposes other than prediction.

A name or a wedding date chosen because it is "auspicious" may end deliberation and shift responsibility for a bad outcome away from the person, and a sign or number is a ready topic between strangers; people act on these systems even when the predictions fail (Kaku, 1975; Lu et al., 2020; Mocan & Yu, 2020).
text.formatted: A name or a wedding date chosen because it is "auspicious" may end deliberation and shift responsibility for a bad outcome away from the person, and a sign or number is a ready topic between strangers; people act on these systems even when the predictions fail <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kaku, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Lu et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Mocan & Yu, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the systems are hard to refute from within.

With nine Personal Years, twelve signs and a two-in-twelve tenchusatsu cycle, a large share of any group's events falls in some meaningful year by chance: about 11% of deaths in Personal Year 9 and about 17% of endings in a tenchusatsu year in our data.
The Abe case is one of the roughly 11% of deaths that fall in a Personal Year 9; the other 89% are not reported as numerological events.
Because sources disagree on the rules (Table 1), a case that fails under one version can succeed under another, and the school can be chosen after the outcome.
text.formatted: Because sources disagree on the rules (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>), a case that fails under one version can succeed under another, and the school can be chosen after the outcome.

text.text: Third, the material is computable, so the answers look objective, and the systems are described as statistics without having been built from counted outcomes.

Fourth, they are sustained commercially: magazine columns, consultations and naming services revise and renew them, as the public dispute between Japanese name-divination schools in the early 1930s already shows.

The only birth-date effects in our data, and in the literature reviewed in Section 2, arise from human institutions or beliefs: the relative-age effect from school years and youth categories, and the fire-horse and dragon-year effects from people acting on the calendar.
The systems have no power to foretell lives.
What power they have is to change behaviour, and so occasionally to fulfil themselves.
The first run of the blind matching test, read on its own, would look like strong evidence for numerology.
Its source was mundane: the reading model, given names and dates of birth, named most people against its instructions, and appears to have shaped readings to their known lives.
When the reading model saw only the numbers, a second route remained.
The judge recognised some persons from the summaries, recalled their dates of birth, and chose the summaries whose recalled dates reproduced the numbers in the reading.

This is the machine equivalent of "hot reading", in which a fortune-teller learns about a client in advance, except that here the knowledge was in the model's training data and neither model was told to use it.
Three lessons follow for research that uses language models as generators or judges.
First, an instruction not to use identifying information does not prevent its use: the reading model named the person in 80% of readings despite the instruction.
Second, removing identifying input from one model does not close the route if another model in the pipeline can recognise the material: a judge's knowledge of the subjects is itself a channel.
Third, the channel can be tested.
Asking the judge to identify each item on its own, before or after the main task, and relating identification to performance, is cheap and diagnostic.
In our data the hits were consistent with identity recall in both samples, and other cues (prominence, summary length, era) remained.
For AI fortune-telling, the implication is that a reading of a person the model knows can draw on the model's knowledge of that person, and the user will experience it as accurate.

Wikidata and Olympedia are incomplete and uneven across countries and periods, and old records heap birth dates on round days; permutation within strata and sensitivity analyses address the structure of birth dates but not every recording error.

The Japanese data lack complete winner lists for 1894-1904, and the compilation of Study 1 miscoded 66 members as in office, which was corrected after the first submission without changing any conclusion.
Several analyses used dummy-variable logit instead of conditional logit.
The timing tests of Registration 3 were effectively computed during a code check before the confirmatory run.
The first blind matching run had a design flaw that the registration did not anticipate.

The identity-recall check was added after the results were known and after informal probes, and is exploratory, although its analyses and reading were registered before it was run; one Japanese member's identification depends on the romanisation rule.
The orb-based variant of the Jupiter rule was not computed.
It used the same judge model as H4 and cannot show which other cues the judge used.
The records show that every registration preceded every dated analysis file, but not the time of data retrieval or of the confirmatory runs of Studies 1 and 2 within 24 October 2026.

Across 33 preregistered tests on legislators, Olympians and laureates, numerology, sun-sign astrology and sanmeigaku did not predict who would rise, when careers would begin or end, or when people would die, while the same design detected a real birth-date effect created by human institutions.

In a blind matching test, language models applying numerology appeared to succeed, first because the reading model named the person and then, by the registered criteria, because the judge recognised the person and recalled the date of birth.
Researchers who use language models as judges should test whether the models know the subjects.
